questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 4 months of fatigue, 6kg weight loss and postural dizziness. BP 96/58 lying, 78/50 standing. There is hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa. Na 128, K 5.8, glucose 3.1.
questions.lead: Which biochemical pattern do you expect on further testing?
options: ACTH high, renin low, aldosterone high
ACTH high, renin high, aldosterone low
ACTH low, renin high, aldosterone low
ACTH low, renin low, aldosterone high
questions.explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency destroys the whole cortex. Cortisol deficiency removes pituitary feedback → ACTH high (and pigmentation, since ACTH and MSH share the POMC precursor). Loss of the zona glomerulosa → aldosterone low, so volume depletion drives renin high. The rule: aldosterone low with renin high = the gland has failed. High aldosterone with low renin is the opposite problem (Conn's).

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has dark urine 2 days after the onset of a sore throat. BP 118/75. Urinalysis: blood 3+, protein 1+. Complement C3 is normal.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Haematuria during the infection (synpharyngitic, 1–2 days) with a normal C3 is IgA nephropathy. Post-streptococcal GN occurs 1–2 weeks after infection with a low C3 that normalises by 6–8 weeks, and usually with hypertension and oedema. Timing plus complement separates them; either alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has an inferior STEMI. BP 86/54, HR 52, JVP elevated, chest clear. ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with ST elevation in V4R.
questions.explanation: V4R elevation confirms right ventricular infarction. The RV becomes acutely preload-dependent, so nitrates (and morphine and diuretics) can cause profound hypotension and are avoided. Management is the opposite of the usual reflex: give fluids to support preload, and proceed to urgent reperfusion. Note the rule is not 'withhold GTN in inferior MI' — it is 'withhold when there is RV involvement'.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is 4 days post laparotomy. Platelets have fallen from 280 to 95 × 10⁹/L. She has been on subcutaneous heparin prophylaxis. There is no bleeding and no thrombosis.
questions.lead: Which feature most argues against heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
options: The magnitude of the platelet fall
questions.explanation: HIT characteristically begins days 5–10 after heparin exposure (earlier only if there was heparin exposure within the preceding 30 days). A fall at day 4 without prior exposure is too early and points to another cause — post-operative haemodilution, sepsis, or drug effect. The other features are all compatible with HIT: a >50% fall fits, thrombosis is common but not required, and surgical patients are at higher risk than medical.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with COPD presents with increasing breathlessness. ABG on 28% oxygen: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 66mmHg, PaO₂ 55mmHg, HCO₃ 30. He is alert and cooperative.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue current therapy and repeat the gas in 4 hours
questions.explanation: Acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure with pH <7.35 in an alert patient who can protect their airway → NIV, which reduces intubation rates and mortality. Intubation is for NIV failure or inability to protect the airway. Escalating FiO₂ risks worsening hypercapnia; target SpO₂ 88–92% in COPD.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman is brought in confused. She is disorientated, inattentive, and her symptoms fluctuate through the day, worse in the evening. She was cognitively normal a week ago. She is on oxybutynin for urinary urgency.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis and the priority action?
options: Delirium; identify and treat the underlying cause including medication review
questions.explanation: Acute onset, fluctuating course, impaired attention defines delirium — dementia is chronic and progressive, in clear consciousness. Priority is finding the cause: infection, medications (oxybutynin is anticholinergic and a common culprit), metabolic derangement, retention, constipation, pain. Management is treating the cause plus non-pharmacological measures; antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress or risk.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to ED after a fall from a roof. GCS is E2 V2 M4. He is maintaining his own airway currently.
questions.lead: What is the GCS total and what does it indicate?
questions.explanation: E2 (opens to pain) + V2 (incomprehensible sounds) + M4 (withdraws from pain) = 8. The classic threshold is GCS ≤8 → intubate, since airway protective reflexes are unreliable — 'GCS 8, intubate' is the aide-memoire. Note that maintaining an airway at this moment does not mean he will continue to, particularly with a deteriorating head injury.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has an anaphylactic reaction to an antibiotic. She has stridor, widespread urticaria and BP 78/44.
options: IM adrenaline 0.5mg (0.5mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh
questions.explanation: IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the only intervention that reverses the immediate life threat, repeated every 5 minutes as needed. Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts with no role in acute reversal — giving them first is the classic fatal delay. IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory shock with specialist involvement, given the arrhythmia risk.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man on apixaban for AF requires an urgent hip hemiarthroplasty after a fractured neck of femur. Last dose was this morning. CrCl is 55 mL/min.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate approach to his anticoagulation?
options: Bridge with therapeutic LMWH once apixaban is stopped
Stop apixaban and delay surgery until the appropriate interruption interval has elapsed, balancing fracture-surgery timing
questions.explanation: Hip fracture surgery is high bleeding risk, so the standard interval is 48 hours from the last apixaban dose with CrCl ≥50 — balanced against the fact that hip fracture outcomes worsen with delay, so this is an explicit multidisciplinary trade-off, not an automatic wait. Bridging is not used with DOACs. Protamine reverses heparin, not apixaban (andexanet alfa is the specific agent, reserved for life-threatening bleeding).

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with haematemesis. BP 92/58, HR 112. He has known oesophageal varices.
questions.lead: Which combination is most appropriate initially?
options: Fluid resuscitation, IV terlipressin (or octreotide), IV antibiotics, and urgent endoscopy
Fluid resuscitation and urgent endoscopy alone
IV proton pump inhibitor and observation
questions.explanation: Variceal bleeding needs four things together: resuscitation, a splanchnic vasoconstrictor (terlipressin or octreotide) to reduce portal pressure, prophylactic antibiotics — which independently reduce mortality and are the component most often forgotten — and endoscopy within 12 hours for band ligation. TIPS is rescue therapy for failed endoscopic control. Aim for a restrictive transfusion threshold (~70g/L); over-transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens bleeding.
